summary: Argues that networks do not need to control jitter in order to support isochronous applications such as real-time audio and video. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This paper says you do not need perfectly even delivery for live calls to work.

questions: do isochronous applications require jitter control
how do networks support live audio and video
subtitle: Networks that control delay and bandwidth are enough for live audio and video.

tldr.problem: People thought networks needed to strictly control jitter (variation in delivery timing) to support live voice and video calls, which seemed to require expensive hardware modifications.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC argues that if a receiver has a buffer and knows the maximum network delay, it can use timestamps and the operating system's own scheduling to deliver data on time, making jitter control redundant.
tldr.outcome: This insight simplified multimedia networking design by showing that delay and bandwidth control alone were sufficient, influenced by the End-to-End Principle.

today: RFC 1257 remains informational and reflects 1991-era thinking about multimedia networking. The principle that jitter control is not required at the network layer has held up, though modern approaches like Quality of Service and buffer management have become more sophisticated.

sections.title: The Jitter Control Question
sections.content:
As networks became faster in the 1990s, researchers wanted to run isochronous applications like voice and video over them. These applications need to produce or process data at regular intervals: a telephone sends voice samples at fixed intervals, and a video codec generates frames at a steady rate.

A common belief was that networks must control jitter (variation in the time between data arrivals) to support these applications, because users notice when audio stutters or video flickers if delivery times are uneven.
sections.eli5: Phone calls and video streaming need steady delivery, and many experts thought the network itself had to guarantee that steadiness.

sections.title: Solving Jitter Without Network Control
sections.content:
The RFC proposes an alternative approach. The network only needs to guarantee a maximum delay (and provide sufficient bandwidth). The receiver can then buffer incoming data and use timestamps to deliver it at the right time, synchronized with the receiver's own clock.

For example, a video receiver could buffer frames and display each one when the timestamp plus the maximum network delay arrives. The operating system wakes the application at regular intervals using clock interrupts, ensuring steady output regardless of whether packets arrived at uniform intervals.
sections.eli5: The receiver waits a bit and then outputs data on a steady clock, like a buffer that smooths out the bumps in delivery.

sections.title: Impact on Network Design
sections.content:
This argument has practical consequences for gigabit networking protocols. If jitter control is not required, then internet protocols for multimedia should only specify control over delay and bandwidth, not jitter.

The RFC notes that most receiving devices already have memory for buffering, unlike telephones of that era. Networks that lack jitter control can still support isochronous applications if the last network switch adds buffering before the final receiver. This insight aligned with the End-to-End Principle, which says that network sophistication should not duplicate functions that end systems can provide themselves.
sections.eli5: Networks only need to promise steady speed and not lose data. The computer on the receiving end handles the rest with its own buffer and clock.

references.text: Mills, D., "Measured Performance of the Network Time Protocol in the Internet System", RFC 1128, UDEL, October 1989.
